clinicalPearls: Altitude illness encompasses a spectrum: acute mountain sickness (AMS, the benign form) and the two life-threatening forms, high-altitude cerebral edema (HACE) and high-altitude pulmonary edema (HAPE) (Harrison 22e p.3754).

AMS is a clinical diagnosis presenting 6-12 h after ascent with nonspecific symptoms (headache, nausea, fatigue, dizziness) and few physical findings; the Lake Louise Scoring System is used for research uniformity (Harrison 22e p.3755).

AMS and HACE are viewed as opposite ends of one neurologic continuum; HACE (not AMS) is an encephalopathy whose hallmarks are ataxia and altered consciousness with diffuse cerebral involvement, typically without focal deficits, and progression can be rapid (Harrison 22e p.3755).

The two most important risk factors for altitude illness are a rapid rate of ascent and a prior history of high-altitude illness; exertion is a risk factor, but lack of physical fitness is not (Harrison 22e p.3755).

Illness is likely above 2500 m but has been documented at 1500-2500 m; in the Everest region about 50% of trekkers ascending above 4000 m over 5+ days develop AMS, rising to 84% with direct flight to 3860 m, whereas HACE and HAPE incidence is far lower (roughly 0.1-4%) (Harrison 22e p.3754).

HAPE is primarily a pulmonary disorder and need not be preceded by AMS; it develops within 2-4 days of arrival and rarely after 4-5 days at the same altitude owing to vascular remodeling and adaptation (Harrison 22e p.3757).

HAPE is a noncardiogenic pulmonary edema with normal pulmonary artery wedge pressure, driven by patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction causing regional overperfusion, capillary pressures above 18 mmHg, and capillary stress failure (Harrison 22e p.3757).

Retinal hemorrhages are common at altitudes of 5000 m or more even without AMS/HACE symptoms; most resolve on descent, but macular hemorrhage can cause devastating, occasionally permanent visual loss (Harrison 22e p.3755, 3759).

Gradual ascent with time for acclimatization is the best preventive measure; a conservative target above 3000 m is graded gain of no more than ~300 m per sleeping-altitude night with an extra acclimatization day every third day of gain (Harrison 22e p.3756).

Sickle cell disease is one of the rare exposures in which altitude can provoke vaso-occlusive crisis, reported even at passes as low as 2500 m; thalassemia has not been linked to high-altitude problems (Harrison 22e p.3759).

Hypertensive patients are not more prone to altitude illness, and most with well-controlled hypertension can be reassured that blood pressure stays relatively stable; antihypertensives should be continued at altitude (Harrison 22e p.3759).

High-altitude cough can be severe enough to cause rib fracture above 5000 m; it is multifactorial (cold dry air plus hypoxia and respiratory water loss), and infection is generally not a common cause (Harrison 22e p.3758).
harrison.pathophysiology: Ascent lowers barometric pressure and thus the partial pressure of inspired oxygen, reducing the pressure gradient driving oxygen diffusion along the oxygen cascade. Hypobaric hypoxia is the central trigger for all forms of altitude illness. The normal struggle response is increased ventilation (the cornerstone of acclimatization) mediated by the carotid bodies; this can produce marked respiratory alkalosis (arterial pH may exceed 7.7 at extreme altitude) and dehydration, with alkalosis blunting ventilatory drive in sleep and causing periodic breathing and hypoxemia. Early acclimatization includes renal carbonic-anhydrase suppression with dilute alkaline urine to correct pH, plus increased sympathetic tone, rising erythropoietin/hemoglobin and red cell mass, greater tissue capillary density and mitochondrial numbers, and elevated 2,3-bisphosphoglycerate. Hypoxia-inducible factor governs transcriptional hypoxia responses; the EPAS1 gene (HIF-2alpha) and EGLN1/PPARA influence adaptation in Tibetan highlanders (lower hemoglobin than Han Chinese or Andeans). In AMS/HACE, raised intracranial pressure, increased sympathetic activity, relative hypoventilation, fluid retention/redistribution, and impaired gas exchange contribute; MRI evidence points to vasogenic (interstitial) cerebral edema, especially in the splenium of the corpus callosum, that may become cytotoxic in severe HACE, with hemosiderin deposits as long-lasting footprints. Impaired cerebral autoregulation with hypoxic vasodilation, altered blood-brain-barrier permeability via histamine, arachidonic acid, and VEGF, and venous outflow obstruction raising capillary pressure all promote edema. HAPE results from patchy hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction with regional overperfusion and capillary stress failure at normal wedge pressure; endothelial dysfunction with reduced nitric oxide availability and elevated endothelin-1, exaggerated sympathetic drive (pulmonary venoconstriction), and impaired transepithelial alveolar fluid clearance are implicated. Inflammation in HAPE is regarded as an epiphenomenon rather than the primary cause, although inflammatory/viral respiratory processes can predispose to it.
infectionMimics: Respiratory tract infection / viral illness (HAPE historically misdiagnosed as viral pneumonia or as a viral illness in reentry HAPE)
Pneumonia (HAPE radiographic opacities simulating pneumonic consolidation)
Bacterial or Giardia enteric infection (high-altitude GI bloating/distension must be distinguished from infectious diarrhea)
nonInfectiousMimics: Cardiogenic pulmonary edema / heart failure (HAPE was historically mistaken for heart failure)
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (another noncardiogenic edema, but lung architecture is preserved in HAPE)
Stroke or TIA unrelated to altitude illness
Subarachnoid hemorrhage, transient global amnesia, delirium, cranial nerve palsy occurring at altitude outside altitude sickness
additionalInvestigations: Clinical assessment with Lake Louise Scoring System (used chiefly for research uniformity)
Pulse oximetry (oxygen saturation; arterial blood gas usually not necessary for HAPE)
Chest radiography (patchy/localized opacities or streaky interstitial edema in HAPE; Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are NOT seen)
Electrocardiography (may show right ventricular strain or hypertrophy in HAPE)
Brain MRI (T2 signal change in white matter and splenium of corpus callosum confirmatory of HACE; hemosiderin deposits as footprints)
Echocardiography (recommended when HAPE occurs below 3000 m or when predisposing cardiopulmonary abnormality is suspected)
Lung ultrasound comet-tail/B-line scoring (sensitive but not specific for HAPE)
redFlags: Ataxia or altered consciousness (hallmarks of HACE) - mandates immediate descent
Any hint of HAPE or HACE mandates descent
Tachypnea and tachycardia at rest as HAPE progresses
Blood-tinged sputum following a dry persistent cough
Disproportionate fall in exercise tolerance, or fatigue/dyspnea at rest as the only initial HAPE signs
Debilitating fatigue consistent with severe AMS on descent from a summit (important risk factor for death in mountaineers)
Papilledema or retinal hemorrhages, especially macular hemorrhage with visual loss
harrison.prognosis: AMS is benign and usually self-limited; once symptoms abate (with or without acetazolamide) the patient may reascend gradually. HACE and HAPE are life-threatening but generally reversible with prompt recognition and descent. In HAPE the lung architecture is typically well preserved with rapid reversibility (radiographic opacities can clear in about 2 days), allowing some patients to reascend slowly after a few days of descent and rest; after HACE, reascent within the same trip may be inadvisable. Severe AMS-related debilitating fatigue on descent is an important predictor of death in mountaineers, and macular hemorrhage can rarely cause permanent visual loss. HACE complicated by globus pallidus lesions has been reported to lead to parkinsonism.
pitfalls: Treating AMS as trivial - symptoms overlap with exhaustion, dehydration, hypothermia, hangover, and hyponatremia, and it can progress to life-threatening HACE.
Relying on pulse oximetry alone to predict AMS during a trek - readings should not be used predictively unless guided by clinical signs.
Assuming HAPE is always preceded by AMS - it is primarily pulmonary and may present without headache or nausea, sometimes only as fatigue and rest dyspnea.
Misreading HAPE chest opacities as pneumonia (cold) or as heart failure - Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are absent in HAPE.
Confusing sudden neurologic events (TIA, stroke, subarachnoid hemorrhage, cranial nerve palsy) at altitude with altitude illness - AMS evolves gradually whereas these typically occur suddenly.
Mistaking reentry HAPE in returning highlanders for a viral illness.
Injudicious prophylactic glucocorticoid use by climbers to boost performance - can be tragic owing to severe side effects, especially with prolonged use.
Overhydration - adequate (not excessive) hydration is intended; potent diuretics such as furosemide should be avoided in HAPE.
Comet-tail/B-line lung ultrasound is sensitive but not specific, since B-lines also appear in individuals who never develop clinical HAPE - clinical correlation is essential.
harrison.severityClassification: AMS is graded clinically as mild versus moderate, a subjective judgment based on headache severity and the presence/severity of nausea, fatigue, and dizziness (the Lake Louise Scoring System, without the sleep score, is used for research). The overall spectrum runs from benign AMS to the life-threatening forms HACE (neurologic, the severe end of the AMS-HACE continuum) and HAPE (pulmonary), which can coexist.
management: Prevent illness through gradual ascent with adequate acclimatisation, using acetazolamide prophylaxis in those at higher risk
For acute mountain sickness halt ascent, rest and treat symptomatically, using acetazolamide to speed acclimatisation and dexamethasone to relieve symptoms
Treat high-altitude cerebral oedema as an emergency with immediate descent, supplemental oxygen and dexamethasone
Treat high-altitude pulmonary oedema with descent, oxygen and a pulmonary vasodilator such as nifedipine
Use a portable hyperbaric chamber and supplemental oxygen when descent is delayed or impossible
Recognise ataxia and altered consciousness as red flags for cerebral oedema mandating urgent evacuation
Advise gradual reascent only after symptoms of acute mountain sickness have resolved
